title: Empedocles
orientation: Empedocles of Acragas combined real scientific discoveries (the corporeal nature of air, centrifugal force, sexual reproduction in plants, a theory of evolution by survival of the fittest) with a religious self-image as a fallen, sinning god undergoing cosmic exile, and with a cosmology of four eternal elements driven by the opposed cosmic forces of Love and Strife. It matters because his four-element theory became the standard ancient chemistry for two thousand years, and because his Love/Strife cosmology offers a 'softened', more balanced answer to the Heraclitus/Parmenides dispute over change.
historical_background: Empedocles, a citizen of Acragas on the south coast of Sicily, flourished about 440 B.C., making him a younger contemporary of Parmenides. He was a democratic politician who was eventually banished, in a Sicilian political climate marked by constant conflict between democratic and tyrannical factions, in which the losing side was often executed or exiled and sometimes intrigued with Persia or Carthage. Legend credited him with miracles (controlling winds, reviving a woman apparently dead for thirty days) and held that he died by leaping into the crater of Mount Etna to prove his divinity.
philosophical_problems: How can the fact of motion and change be reconciled with Parmenides' arguments against coming-to-be and passing-away?
Is the natural world governed by purpose, or only by chance and necessity?
What are the basic, irreducible constituents ('elements') of physical reality?
What forces or principles explain why the elements sometimes combine and sometimes separate?

philosophers_discussed.name: Empedocles
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Central subject: proposed earth, air, fire, and water as four everlasting elements, combined and separated by the opposed cosmic forces of Love and Strife in an endless cycle; also a scientist (discoverer of air as a distinct substance, of centrifugal force, and of a crude evolutionary theory) and a self-proclaimed fallen god undergoing purificatory exile.

schools_discussed: Orphism and Pythagoreanism (as the main influence on Empedocles' religious doctrines)
The Italian school of medicine (founded by Empedocles)

core_concepts.name: The four elements (earth, air, fire, water)
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Empedocles proposed that everything is made from just four everlasting basic substances -- earth, air, fire, and water -- mixed together in different proportions, rather than from a single substance as the Milesians and Heraclitus had thought.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Empedocles' doctrine that earth, air, fire, and water are each everlasting and unchanging in themselves, but can be mixed in varying proportions by the opposed forces of Love and Strife to produce all the changing compound substances observed in the world.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Russell calls this a 'statesmanlike compromise' among the Milesians' and Heraclitus's single-substance theories, and notes that 'the chemistry of the ancients stopped dead at this point,' remaining the standard framework until the rise of Islamic alchemy centuries later.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Original to Empedocles, though the term 'element' itself was not used by him.
examples: All complex substances in the world as varying mixtures of the four elements
competing_positions: Thales' water, Anaximenes' air, and Heraclitus's fire as single primal substances
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Remained the basic ancient and medieval theory of matter for roughly two thousand years, until superseded by early chemistry.

core_concepts.name: Love and Strife as cosmic forces
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Empedocles held that the four elements are combined by a force called Love and separated by an opposed force called Strife, and that the history of the universe is a repeating cycle in which first Love, then Strife, gains the upper hand.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Two primitive, elemental forces, ranked by Empedocles alongside earth, air, fire, and water themselves, that respectively unite and separate the elements; their alternating dominance produces a cosmic cycle including a 'Golden Age' when Love was completely victorious and an opposite extreme when Strife is wholly dominant.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Provides a 'softened' alternative to Heraclitus's doctrine that strife alone produces change: for Empedocles it is the interplay of two opposed principles, not strife by itself, that generates the world's changes, addressing Parmenides' objections to change while still accounting for motion.
examples: The Golden Age, when Love was completely victorious and men worshipped only the Cyprian Aphrodite
Plato's summary in the Sophist, contrasting the 'severer' Ionian/Heraclitean view of perpetual strife with the 'gentler' Sicilian view (Empedocles) of alternating Love and Strife
competing_positions: Heraclitus's view that strife alone, without a counterbalancing unifying force, produces the world's harmony
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly modeled on, and named after, the goddess of Love (Aphrodite) and a personified Strife; described within a cyclical mythic framework including a Golden Age.

core_concepts.name: Rejection of purpose: chance and necessity
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Empedocles believed the changes in the world are not directed toward any goal or purpose; they happen simply because of Chance and Necessity acting on the elements, moved by Love and Strife.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Empedocles' doctrine that cosmic change is governed 'not by any purpose, but only by Chance and Necessity,' including a crude evolutionary account in which countless random combinations of body parts arose and only certain viable forms survived.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Russell singles this out as making Empedocles 'more scientific' than Parmenides, Plato, and Aristotle in this particular respect, prefiguring later mechanistic (rather than teleological) explanations of nature, including the atomists' fully mechanistic cosmology in the following chapters.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Part of Empedocles' cosmological and biological speculation, including his fantastic proto-evolutionary account of early monstrous life-forms.
examples: Early 'countless tribes of mortal creatures... with all manner of forms': heads without necks, solitary limbs seeking union, hybrid ox-human creatures
Only certain combinations proving viable and surviving, an early anticipation of survival of the fittest
competing_positions: Anaxagoras's introduction of Mind (nous) as a directing cause (treated in the next chapter), and the general teleological tendency of Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Anticipates, however fantastically, the later Darwinian idea of natural selection acting on random variation.

core_concepts.name: Empedocles' scientific discoveries
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Empedocles proved experimentally that air is a real, distinct substance (using a water-clock/bucket experiment), observed a form of centrifugal force, understood that the moon shines by reflected light and (probably) that the sun does too, and knew that solar eclipses are caused by the moon passing in front of the sun.
core_concepts.precise_definition: A set of empirical discoveries credited to Empedocles: air as a separate corporeal substance (demonstrated via the clepsydra/water-clock experiment), centrifugal force (a whirled cup of water does not spill), sex in plants, the reflected light of the moon (and probably the sun), the finite (though imperceptibly fast) speed of light, and the lunar cause of solar eclipses (learned, Russell suggests, from Anaxagoras).
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Illustrates, for Russell, the genuine 'scientific vigour' of the pre-Socratic period, later matched by his own foundation of the influential Italian school of medicine, which affected the whole subsequent tendency of Greek scientific and philosophical thought.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Empedocles' own reported experiments and writings.
examples: The clepsydra (water-clock) experiment showing air resists water's entry into an inverted vessel
A whirled cup of water not spilling, demonstrating centrifugal force
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: The medical school he founded influenced both Plato and Aristotle, according to Burnet.

key_distinctions: The four permanent elements (earth, air, fire, water) versus the temporary compound substances formed from them
Teleological explanation (purpose) versus explanation by Chance and Necessity
Empedocles' scientific work versus his religious/prophetic self-conception, which Russell treats as inconsistent with each other
connections_to_earlier_philosophers: Empedocles' four-element theory directly resolves the single-substance disputes of the Milesians and Heraclitus (water, air, fire); his cosmology is explicitly framed by Russell, via a quotation from Plato's Sophist, as a 'softening' of Heraclitus's doctrine of strife; his religious self-conception draws on Pythagorean and Orphic doctrines of transmigration and purification (Chapter III); his cosmology 'wished to explain motion while taking account of the arguments of Parmenides' (Chapter V).
connections_to_later_philosophers: His discovery of the lunar cause of solar eclipses is linked to Anaxagoras (next chapter but one); Russell notes his medical school influenced both Plato and Aristotle; his chance-and-necessity cosmology anticipates the fully mechanistic explanations of the atomists (Chapter IX).
political_social_context: Sicilian cities, including Acragas, were marked by chronic conflict between democratic and tyrannical factions, with exiled leaders sometimes intriguing with Persia or Carthage; Empedocles himself was a democratic politician before his banishment.
religion_science_culture_context: Empedocles' religious views are, in Russell's summary, 'in the main, Pythagorean': he describes a Golden Age of pure worship of Aphrodite without animal sacrifice, presents himself alternately as an 'immortal god' honored by crowds and as a fallen 'daemon' undergoing a thirty-thousand-year cosmic exile for an unspecified sin (perhaps as trivial as eating beans or laurel leaves), and anticipates Plato's cave allegory, which Russell traces to Orphic origins.
russell_presentation: Russell frames Empedocles as another instance of the mixture of 'philosopher, prophet, man of science, and charlatan' already seen in Pythagoras, and insists on treating his science, his philosophy (the four elements and Love/Strife), and his religion separately because 'they are not consistent with each other.' He credits Empedocles with real scientific achievements (the corporeal nature of air, centrifugal force, sex in plants, a fantastical but genuinely proto-evolutionary account of the origin of species) and judges his rejection of purpose in favor of Chance and Necessity to be, in this respect, 'more scientific' than Parmenides, Plato, or Aristotle. At the same time, Russell recounts with evident amusement the more grandiose and superstitious sides of Empedocles' self-presentation -- as a wonder-working immortal god on the one hand, and as a guilt-ridden exiled 'daemon' on the other -- without endorsing either. He treats the Love/Strife cosmology as historically significant chiefly for how it engages with, and softens, the Heraclitus/Parmenides dispute over change.
key_takeaways: Empedocles proposed earth, air, fire, and water as four eternal elements, mixed in different proportions to form all changing compound substances -- the basic theory of matter in antiquity for roughly two thousand years.
He explained cosmic change through the opposed forces of Love (uniting) and Strife (separating), cycling between a Golden Age of total Love and an opposite extreme of total Strife.
He rejected purpose in nature, attributing all change to Chance and Necessity, including a fantastical proto-evolutionary theory in which only viable combinations of body parts survived.
He made genuine empirical discoveries: air as a distinct substance (via the water-clock experiment), centrifugal force, sex in plants, and the lunar cause of solar eclipses.

He also presented himself religiously (in Pythagorean/Orphic terms) both as an immortal, wonder-working god and as a sinning 'daemon' undergoing a long cosmic exile -- a religious self-conception Russell treats as inconsistent with his scientific work.
Russell judges his rejection of teleology (purpose) as making him, in this respect, more scientific than Parmenides, Plato, or Aristotle.
study_notes:
The organizing tension in this chapter, which Russell states outright, is that Empedocles' science and his religion 'are not consistent with each other' -- so read the chapter in the three parts Russell himself proposes (science, cosmology/philosophy, religion) rather than looking for one unified 'Empedoclean' worldview. The Love/Strife cosmology is best understood as a direct response to the Heraclitus-versus-Parmenides debate from the two previous chapters: Empedocles wants real motion and change (against Parmenides) but does not want Heraclitus's picture of strife alone as the engine of everything, so he adds Love as a genuinely separate, opposed principle.

It is also worth noticing how much genuine scientific method appears here (a real experiment with a water-clock to prove air is a substance) sitting right next to material that looks like religious extravagance (self-proclaimed godhood, a fantastic tale of cosmic exile for eating beans). Russell does not try to resolve this tension or explain it away; he simply presents it as characteristic of the period, continuing the pattern already seen with Pythagoras.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Empedocles' idea that everything is made from just four basic, everlasting ingredients: earth, air, fire, and water, mixed in different amounts.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Empedocles' doctrine that earth, air, fire, and water are each eternal and unchanging, combined and separated by Love and Strife to produce the world's changing compound substances; the standard theory of matter in antiquity until early chemistry.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Two opposing cosmic forces Empedocles believed drive all change: Love brings the elements together, and Strife pulls them apart.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Two primitive forces, treated as substances on a level with the four elements, whose alternating dominance in a repeating cosmic cycle explains the combination and separation of the elements, and hence all coming-to-be and passing-away.

questions.prompt: What four substances did Empedocles propose as the everlasting basic elements of the world?
questions.explanation: Russell calls this a 'statesmanlike compromise' among the earlier single-substance theories of the Milesians and Heraclitus.

questions.prompt: What two cosmic forces did Empedocles say combine and separate the four elements?
questions.answer: Love (which combines/unites the elements) and Strife (which separates them).
questions.explanation: Their alternating dominance produces a repeating cosmic cycle, including a Golden Age when Love was completely victorious.

questions.prompt: What experiment did Empedocles use to demonstrate that air is a real, corporeal substance?
questions.answer: The water-clock (clepsydra) experiment: when the vessel's opening is covered, air inside prevents water from entering; uncovering it lets air escape and water flow in.
questions.explanation: This is presented by Russell as Empedocles' most important scientific contribution.

questions.prompt: Contrast Empedocles' explanation of cosmic change (Love and Strife) with Heraclitus's explanation (strife alone), as summarized by Plato and quoted by Russell.
questions.answer: Heraclitus (the 'severer' view) holds that strife alone, unopposed, produces the world's unity and change. Empedocles (the 'gentler' view) holds that both Love and Strife are needed, alternating in dominance, so that unity and plurality both result from the interplay of two opposed principles rather than from conflict alone.
questions.explanation: Russell quotes Plato's Sophist to make this exact contrast explicit.

questions.prompt: Which pre-Socratic philosopher rejected purpose in favor of Chance and Necessity, and proposed a proto-evolutionary theory in which only viable combinations of body parts survived?
questions.explanation: Russell judges this rejection of teleology to make Empedocles, in this respect, more scientific than Parmenides, Plato, and Aristotle.

quiz.related_concept: The four elements (earth, air, fire, water)

quiz.prompt: What two opposed forces did Empedocles say combine and separate the elements?
quiz.explanation: Love combines the elements; Strife separates them, in an alternating cosmic cycle.

quiz.prompt: What experiment did Empedocles use to demonstrate that air is a distinct, corporeal substance?
options: A water-clock (clepsydra) showing air keeps water from entering a covered vessel
quiz.explanation: Russell quotes Empedocles' own description of a girl's water-clock experiment demonstrating that air occupies space.

quiz.prompt: Empedocles believed the changes and forms found in nature are directed by purpose.
quiz.explanation: Empedocles held that change is governed only by Chance and Necessity, not by purpose.
quiz.related_concept: Rejection of purpose: chance and necessity

quiz.prompt: According to Plato's Sophist, as quoted by Russell, how does the 'gentler' Sicilian view (Empedocles) of cosmic unity and plurality differ from the 'severer' Ionian (Heraclitean) view?
options: It denies that unity and plurality both exist
It holds that peace/unity (Love) and strife/plurality alternate, rather than strife alone producing everything
It rejects the existence of any cosmic forces at all
It claims only unity is real, denying plurality entirely
quiz.explanation: The 'gentler' view admits 'a relaxation and alternation' of peace (Love/Aphrodite) and strife, rather than insisting, as the 'severer' Heraclitean view does, on perpetual strife alone.
quiz.related_concept: Love and Strife as cosmic forces

quiz.prompt: According to legend, Empedocles died by leaping into the crater of ____ to prove he was a god.
quiz.explanation: This legend is recorded, with the mocking couplet Russell quotes, about Empedocles' death.

quiz.prompt: From what city did Empedocles come?
quiz.explanation: Empedocles was a citizen of Acragas, on the south coast of Sicily.

Explains how the theory accommodates Parmenidean concerns about change
Clear structure and use of evidence
